newsitem.title: USA: High zinc premiums are short-term - Big River.
newsitem.headline: High zinc premiums are short-term - Big River.

text.p: Zinc premiums have climbed higher in the United States to cover the cost of importing more metal, but premiums are set to fall closer to their traditional levels, according to Ed Schmidt of Big River Zinc.
"I would like to see the premium stay at six cents, but I don't think it will stay there," Schmidt told delegates of the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries round table here.
Big River was recently taken over by Korea Zinc, one of the world's biggest producers.
Physical zinc in the United States is priced by adding a premium to London Metal Exchange cash zinc price. The present premium is about 6.0 to 6.5 cents per pound.
Schmidt said premiums of six cents and above were "short- term" and will fall to the average rate of 4.5 cents.

Schmidt argued that the cost of importing "opportunistic" metal - zinc from countries which normally don't export large volumes to the U.S. - was about 6 cents per pound, which is why premiums rose because metal was tight at present.
But in some cases, premiums for importing metal could be much lower if inland freight costs are reduced.
This year the U.S. is forecast to import 539,000 tonnes from Canada, 104,000 tonnes from Mexico, and 137,000 tonnes in total from Australia, Finland, Norway, Peru and Spain.
Brasil, seen as an opportunistic supplier, was expected to export 39,000 tonnes to the U.S. this year, with 10,000 tonnes from other countries.

Total U.S. imports in 1996 will be 835,000 tonnes with U.S. consumption forecast to reach 1.235 million tonnes, Schmidt said. Some 25,000 tonnes will be sold from the U.S. government stockpile. U.S. production is about 380,000 tonnes.
U.S. zinc production has remained flat for several years while demand continues to grow as new galvanizing lines are being built, consuming an extra 5,000 to 10,000 tonnes a year per line.

A good indication of current premiums were the U.S. Mint which buys special high grade metal for making penny coins, and the government stockpile, which sells prime western and high grade metal. The difference in the price is usually about 2.5 cents per pound, Schmidt said.
But trader Morton Schwarz of Trademet told delegates, "It's highly unlikely we will see a reversing in the upward bias in premiums this year."

Schwarz cautioned that people in the zinc market have been lulled into a false sense of security because of weak zinc prices on LME. "The price doldrums are about to change and the cold zinc winds are about to be ignited," he said.
Russian metal availability has fallen and is now sold at only a $5 to $10 per tonne discount to LME cash, compared to a $10 per tonne premium paid for Western special high grade.
"Chinese demand for zinc is also understated," Schwarz said.
Refined zinc stocks are falling, and although most expected a zinc concentrates surplus over the next 12 months, the magnitidue of it will be much less, at just 40,000 to 100,000 tonnes.
Schwarz said this was manageable and will leave treatment charges for concentrates in 1997 largely unchanged at $190 to $195 per tonne basis LME price of $1,000 per tonne.
